transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-20
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood Product), Marcus Daly (CTO, Oceana), Leila Moreno (Platform), Chris Park (Security), Ana Ruiz (DevOps)

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. quick agenda — we'll run through how Redwood handles rate limits, org and project keys for multi-tenant setups, show the console and API snippets, then leave time for security questions. Priya is gonna drive the demo.

[00:18] Marcus Daly: Sounds good. I just want to make sure we cover per-tenant quotas, and how we can limit noisy tenants without impacting the rest of our customers. also curious about key rotation and audit logs.

[00:30] Priya Rao: Yep, perfect. quick note — apologies if audio is a bit rough, the auto-transcript sometimes munges acronyms like K V cache as 'K V chase' — I'll try to call those out.

[00:45] Priya Rao: Alright I'm sharing my screen, console first. this is the org view — you can see we have org-wide rate limits, and then project-scoped keys that inherit or override policies. so for a multi-tenant app you'd create an org, then create projects for each customer, and issue project keys per tenant.

[01:10] Leila Moreno: so project keys are what we'd give to each of our customers? or do you recommend a proxy key pattern?

[01:20] Priya Rao: good question. both patterns are supported. common approach: issue project keys per tenant if you want per-tenant throttling and visibility. if you want to front with your own proxy, you can use a service account key for your proxy and set per-route policies. either way you get usage metrics per project in the console.

[01:40] Priya Rao: here is the rate-limits page — policies are rules you can attach at org, project, or route-level. you can set token-based limits (tokens/minute), request-per-minute, or concurrency limits. Important: we support both hard throttles and soft warnings with sampled traces for debugging.

[02:05] Marcus Daly: can we do burst allowances? we have tenants that spike occasionally with batch jobs.

[02:12] Priya Rao: yes — you can define a sustained rate plus a burst bucket. think of it as a leaky bucket with configurable burst size. we also have a burst quota pool that can be shared across projects if you want a global buffer.

[02:30] Chris Park: how does this interact with Dedicated vs Hosted? we need to know if a noisy tenant on hosted could affect others or if Dedicated isolates them.

[02:40] Priya Rao: good point. on Hosted we enforce tenant policies in the control plane and runtime; noisy tenants will be throttled per policy, but resource contention is still possible at extreme loads — that's where Dedicated helps: you get dedicated GPU pools and stronger isolation. we also support routing policies so critical tenants can hit dedicated capacity.

[02:58] Samir Patel: adding — for customers with strict SLAs, we recommend Dedicated or Private deployments. but for most multi-tenant apps Hosted + project keys + strict rate policies is enough.

[03:15] Jordan Lee: quick note on billing — project-level usage rolls up and you can map charges to projects for internal cost allocation.

[03:30] Priya Rao: switching to API. here's how you create a project key via API: POST /v1/orgs/{org_id}/projects with key creation flags; keys are scoped to project and can be rotated via the keys endpoint. I'm pasting an example in chat — excuse the transcript, it may mangle backticks.

[04:05] Ana Ruiz: rotation — can we automate rotation via our KMS? we use AWS KMS and prefer to keep secrets out of the Redwood control plane if possible.

[04:15] Priya Rao: yes — you can integrate with customer-managed KMS for key wrapping in Private deployments. for Hosted we support Bring-Your-Own-KMS via cloud KMS and HSM integrations on enterprise plans; there's also envelope encryption so actual data keys are encrypted under your KMS.

[04:40] Chris Park: about audit logging — does Redwood log key usage and admin changes? we need immutable logs for audits.

[04:50] Priya Rao: yes we emit admin audit logs (key creation/rotation/policies) and usage logs per request including key id, route, and token counts. logs can be exported to your SIEM via S3, GCS, or streaming connectors. retention and export options are configurable for enterprise customers.

[05:15] Marcus Daly: can you show a sample rate-limit rule that allows an internal service more leeway than external tenants?

[05:25] Priya Rao: sure — here's a route-level override attached to /api/chat route — internal_service_key gets 2000 tokens/min, default project keys get 200 tokens/min. you can match on header, IP, or key id.

[05:45] Priya Rao: also worth calling out metrics — per-key token counts, 95th latency, and throttle events are shown. you can create alerts when throttle rates exceed a threshold so ops can investigate.

[06:05] Leila Moreno: what's the expected latency hit for enforcing per-key throttles? we worry about extra hop time.

[06:12] Priya Rao: enforcement is done in the edge control plane and optimized in the runtime — typically sub-millisecond overhead for rate checks. the bigger latency factors are model selection and batching. Rate checks are cached for a few seconds to avoid roundtrips.

[06:35] Jordan Lee: quick product note — Optimize recommendations can suggest which workloads would benefit from stricter client-side throttling or batching to reduce per-token cost.

[06:50] Marcus Daly: what about quota resets — calendar-based or rolling window?

[06:55] Priya Rao: both. you can choose fixed window (calendar) or sliding window semantics per policy. sliding windows are better for smoothing spikes.

[07:10] Priya Rao: now i'll demonstrate creating a project, issuing a key, and setting a custom policy. give me a sec.

[07:30] Priya Rao: creating project 'oceana-prod'... key created — notice the UI shows key fingerprint, created_by, and assigned policy. we mask the key so ops can't accidentally copy it; you can download the private key material once.

[07:50] Ana Ruiz: can we disable key download after issuance? we have strict controls.

[07:55] Priya Rao: yes — there's a disable-download flag. best practice is to rotate and revoke if needed.

[08:10] Leila Moreno: for our multi-tenant architecture, we might put a long-lived service account in front and mint short-lived project keys for downstream requests. is that supported?

[08:20] Priya Rao: yes — short-lived keys via the token service (JWT) are supported; you can mint ephemeral tokens with TTLs and scope them to a project. that's common when you want ephemeral credentials.

[08:40] Marcus Daly: curious about the console's enforcement visibility. how granular are the logs? can we see per-request token consumption?

[08:50] Priya Rao: per-request metadata includes tokens_consumed, model, sequence_length, project_id, route, and key_id. you can filter and export. note the transcript auto-tool sometimes spells 'tokens' as 'tockens' — sorry for that.

[09:12] Priya Rao: switching now to a demo of throttling rules in action — i'll run a small script that simulates a tenant spike and show the throttle events in the console live.

[09:30] [screen shows spike graph]

[09:34] Priya Rao: you can see throttle events pop up, and the policy shows which requests were dropped vs delayed. we also sample a subset of throttled requests for debugging with request traces.

[09:50] Chris Park: when a request is dropped, is there a standard response code? and do you return headers indicating remaining quota?

[09:58] Priya Rao: yes — we return 429 for hard throttles and 202 for soft-deferred responses depending on policy. headers include x-rw-quota-remaining and x-rw-quota-reset. you can customize header names if you proxy through.

[10:15] Marcus Daly: is there SDK support to auto-honor backoff headers?

[10:20] Priya Rao: our SDKs include retry/backoff helpers that respect quota headers. we also provide examples for exponential backoff with jitter.

[10:35] Jordan Lee: ok jumping to a common security topic — SAML SSO, RBAC, and how admin permissions map to policies.

[10:45] Priya Rao: admin roles are RBAC driven — org owners, project admins, read-only viewers. SAML/SSO maps to these roles; you can also have SCIM provisioning.

[11:00] Chris Park: does RBAC extend to who can change rate policies? we want a separation of duties — devs can view but only ops can change quotas.

[11:08] Priya Rao: absolutely — policy CRUD is gated by role. you can create a policy change workflow where changes require approval; we also log policy change events in the audit trail.

[11:25] Ana Ruiz: for Private deployments, where does the control plane live and how are policies enforced?

[11:32] Priya Rao: in Private we offer a customer-managed control plane; enforcement can be local to your network with connectors to Redwood's updates. that way policy decisions and key material never leave your VPC unless you opt in.

[11:50] Marcus Daly: good. encryption — you mentioned envelope encryption earlier. would raw request bodies ever be accessible to Redwood if we use BYO KMS?

[11:58] Priya Rao: with BYO KMS and Private deployment, customer data keys are encrypted under your KMS; the control plane doesn't have plaintext key material. Hosted with BYO KMS also uses envelope encryption but there are more managed defaults — we can walk through the exact threat model in the security deep-dive.

[12:20] Leila Moreno: is there a limit to number of project keys per org? we will have thousands of tenants potentially.

[12:27] Priya Rao: we handle thousands of keys — there's paging and lifecycle tools for key management. for very large fleets we recommend programmatic key rotation and provisioning APIs which we demonstrated here.

[12:40] Jordan Lee: Samir, any product caveats to call out?

[12:44] Samir Patel: just that rate policies are very flexible but complexity can grow. recommend standardizing a small set of policy templates and using inheritance: org defaults, then project overrides. Optimize can suggest policy tightening where appropriate.

[13:00] Marcus Daly: could Optimize suggest per-tenant quotas based on historical usage?

[13:06] Priya Rao: yes — Optimize analyzes traffic and suggests bucket sizes, burst allowances, and which tenants should be moved to Dedicated to avoid noisy neighbor issues.

[13:25] Leila Moreno: demo looks good. can we talk about per-route limits too? we have some endpoints expensive in tokens.

[13:33] Priya Rao: per-route limits are important — you can set route-specific token multipliers or hard caps by route. also set model-specific limits so heavy model calls are curtailed.

[13:50] Marcus Daly: how do you handle model fallback when capacity is constrained? we sometimes want to hit cheaper smaller models instead.

[13:58] Priya Rao: Redwood supports automatic fallback policies: when a model is at capacity you can fallback to a compatible variant (e.g., quantized or smaller family) and still serve requests. fallback can be prioritized per project.

[14:15] Chris Park: do fallbacks affect billing? we need to know cost attribution.

[14:20] Priya Rao: billing records the model actually served; you can set cost caps per project and trigger throttles or fallbacks to keep spend under control.

[14:35] Jordan Lee: taking a few live questions from Ana about implementation.

[14:40] Ana Ruiz: what's the per-request header overhead for tracing and quotas? we want to avoid huge headers.

[14:46] Priya Rao: headers are minimal — key id, quota remaining, and trace id. if you enable heavy tracing you'll get additional metadata but that's optional.

[15:02] Priya Rao: jumping ahead a bit — showing how to create a policy via API: payload includes scope, metric (tokens/min), window type, burst, action (throttle/drop/defer), and optional sample_rate for debug traces.

[15:25] Marcus Daly: sample_rate — can we selectively sample only throttled requests?

[15:30] Priya Rao: yes, you can set sample_on='throttled' which will only keep traces for throttled requests. that's helpful for debugging without data deluge.

[15:45] Leila Moreno: ok one more on automation — do you offer Terraform provider or IaC to manage org/projects/policies?

[15:52] Priya Rao: yes — we have a Terraform provider and REST APIs for everything in the console. provisioning at scale is a supported pattern.

[16:05] Jordan Lee: security deeper question from Chris — KMS, HSM, and key wrapping.

[16:12] Chris Park: we need to know if private keys ever land in Redwood-managed hardware.

[16:18] Priya Rao: short answer: with BYO KMS and Private, no. with Hosted we offer BYO KMS where keys are wrapped but the envelope flow requires the control plane for orchestration; we'll cover exact flows in the security session. we also support HSM-backed signing for enterprise.

[16:40] Marcus Daly: good, that's key for us. any limits on the rate of key rotations? we might rotate daily.

[16:46] Priya Rao: programmatic rotation is fine; the system supports high rotation rates but operationally we recommend ephemeral tokens for high churn patterns.

[17:00] Priya Rao: switching now to a quick script run — i'll fire requests from a simulated tenant to show backoff headers and SDK behavior.

[17:15] [script running — console shows headers: x-rw-quota-remaining: 0 / reset in 00:01:30]

[17:24] Priya Rao: see the 429s returning with header info; SDK retries honor backoff. in the console you can see which key triggered the throttle and the exact rule name.

[17:40] Marcus Daly: can we set different billing units — e.g., bill per-request instead of per-token for certain routes?

[17:48] Priya Rao: you can map billing metrics to different billing units per route; for example some customers prefer request-based billing for short chat messages. we'll help map usage to pricing models.

[18:05] Leila Moreno: any concerns about data residency if logs are exported for audits? we need EU-only retention for some work.

[18:12] Priya Rao: we support region-restricted log exports and EU-only retention for enterprise accounts; Private deployment gives you the most control.

[18:30] Samir Patel: minor note — Optimize can run offline analysis on historical logs to recommend region placement and cost/perf tradeoffs.

[18:45] Jordan Lee: ok time check — about 28 minutes in. want to open the floor to any final security or integration questions, then recap next steps.

[19:00] Chris Park: two items — we need SOC 2 scope doc and an architecture threat model for Private deployment.

[19:08] Jordan Lee: we'll send SOC2 summary and schedule the threat-model workshop. added to next steps.

[19:20] Marcus Daly: one more on alerting — can we get Cortex/Prometheus metrics or do you push internally?

[19:28] Priya Rao: we export Prometheus metrics and can stream to your metrics backend; plus you get alerts through webhooks and integrations with PagerDuty.

[19:40] Leila Moreno: for pilot sizing — what's a recommended pilot to validate throttling behavior?

[19:46] Priya Rao: common pilot: 1-week test, 50k tokens/day across 5 test tenants with synthetic spikes. that reveals noisy neighbor behavior and validates your policy templates.

[20:05] Ana Ruiz: we'll do that. Marcus will confirm the traffic profile.

[20:12] Marcus Daly: yeah we'll capture sample traffic and share.

[20:20] Jordan Lee: quick recap — Priya will send policy examples and screenshots, Jordan will share pricing and pilot contract, Chris and Redwood security to meet 26th for deep-dive. Marcus to confirm pilot traffic.

[20:38] Leila Moreno: any notes on rollback if pilot shows issues? can we suspend keys/roll back policies?

[20:45] Priya Rao: yes — you can immediately revoke keys, disable projects, or revert policies. there's a policy audit log and change history to revert.

[21:00] Marcus Daly: one last nit — in our stack we'd probably prefer short-lived tokens minted by our identity service. earlier you mentioned TTLs; what's max TTL?

[21:10] Priya Rao: you can set TTL down to a second and up to 30 days for longer-lived tokens; recommend short TTLs for tenants.

[21:25] Jordan Lee: ok looks like we're near wrap. thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the items in the next steps.

[21:35] Chris Park: thanks, appreciate the clarity.

[21:40] Marcus Daly: appreciate the demo.

[21:45] [meeting closes]

Notes on transcript quality: auto-transcript had intermittent errors (acronyms, K V cache spelled odd); speaker labels largely correct though some overlap.

End of transcript.
